intro.heading_en: The Slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha
intro.carita: Prathama Carita (the first episode). In the recitation tradition its presiding form is Mahākālī; this is the Gita Press viniyoga, not a statement of the Purāṇa text.
intro.summary: Mārkaṇḍeya promises the story of Sāvarṇi, the eighth Manu (1.1–3). King Suratha, betrayed by his ministers, rides alone into the forest and reaches the hermitage of the sage Medhas (1.4–11). Still brooding over his lost city, elephant and treasury (1.12–16), he meets Samādhi, a merchant thrown out by his own wife and sons, who cannot stop worrying about them either (1.17–34). Together they ask Medhas why their minds cling to what has rejected them, though they see the fault (1.35–45). Medhas answers that every creature has knowledge, yet all are bound by mamatā, and that the cause is Mahāmāyā, who deludes even the wise, who is the knowledge that liberates and the cause of bondage (1.46–58). Asked who she is (1.59–62), he tells how, at the end of an age, the demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha, born from the wax of Viṣṇu’s ears while he slept, rose to kill Brahmā; Brahmā praised the Goddess as Viṣṇu’s Yoganidrā (1.63–87); she left Viṣṇu’s body, he woke, fought them for five thousand years, and, when the deluded demons offered him a boon, chose their death and slew them on his thighs, where the flood had not reached (1.88–104).
intro.forms: Mahāmāyā, the power that binds and releases (1.55–58); Yoganidrā, the sleep of Viṣṇu (1.54, 1.66–71); Tāmasī, the dark Goddess who leaves Viṣṇu’s body (1.89); and, in Brahmā’s hymn, Svāhā, Svadhā and the syllable (1.73–74), the night of dissolution — Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Moharātri (1.79) — and the mild and the terrible at once (1.80–82).
intro.significance: The frame story poses the question the whole text answers: why knowing is not enough to be free. The first battle is not fought by the Goddess at all: her act is to withdraw from Viṣṇu, so that the god who sustains the world can wake. The demons are destroyed by the same delusion that held the king and the merchant: they offer their enemy a boon.
intro.grammar: Narrative perfects (उवाच, बभूव, ददर्श) and aorists (अभूत्, अद्राक्षीत्); long sentences carried over verse boundaries in the dialogue (1.12–16, 1.22–24, 1.51–55); genitives of the speaker with verbs of hearing (गदतो मम, 1.2); gerundives (कार्यः, 1.54); passives of causatives (सम्मोह्यते, 1.55); and, in Brahmā’s hymn, the second person: त्वम् with nominative predicates, vocatives, and feminine stems in -ā, -ī and -ti.
intro.teaching: Literally, a king and a merchant are consoled by a sage, and a god wakes to kill two demons. As teaching, the chapter says that attachment (mamatā) is not a private weakness but the working of the power that keeps the world in being; that the same power, as knowledge (vidyā), is the cause of liberation (1.57); and that she is not reached by argument but by praise and surrender — Brahmā, helpless on the lotus, does not fight; he praises.
themes: Mamatā and moha: knowing and still clinging
Mahāmāyā as bondage and as liberation
Praise (stuti) as the act that turns events
The frame of the Manvantara: grace inside history

conclusion.narrative: Two men who have lost everything, a king to his ministers and a merchant to his family, find that losing things has not loosened their hold on them. Medhas names the power behind that hold — Mahāmāyā — and, to show who she is, tells the first of the three stories: Brahmā’s praise of Yoganidrā, her withdrawal from the sleeping Viṣṇu, and the death of Madhu and Kaiṭabha. The chapter ends with a promise: more of her power is still to be told (1.104).

constructions: The perfect and the aorist as the narrative past (उवाच, बभूव, अभूत्, अद्राक्षीत्).
The speaker in the genitive with verbs of hearing (निशामय … गदतो मम, 1.2).
Long periodic sentences carried across several ślokas (1.12–16, 1.22–24, 1.51–55); the anvaya joins them.
Passive of a causative with an instrumental agent (तया सम्मोह्यते जगत्, 1.55).
The gerundive of obligation with न (विस्मयः न कार्यः, 1.54).
Hymn style: त्वम् with a predicate nominative, repeated in series (त्वं स्वाहा त्वं स्वधा …, 1.73), feminine vocatives, and compounds of praise.
Pūrvarūpa (-e/-o + a → avagraha) and -aḥ → -o are the commonest sandhis of the chapter.
insights: Attachment is a power, not only a fault: the wise are bound by the same Mahāmāyā as the birds (1.49–55).
The power that binds is the power that frees: she is vidyā and the cause of liberation, and also the cause of bondage (1.57–58).
The Goddess is eternal and unborn, yet is said to ‘arise’ whenever she appears for the gods’ purposes (1.64–65).
Even Viṣṇu, the sustainer, is subject to her: his waking is her withdrawal (1.88–90).
Brahmā’s hymn names her as everything that is — creation, sustenance and dissolution (1.75–77) — and as both gentle and terrible (1.80–82).
conclusion.srividya: The chapter shares names with the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) — Mahāmāyā (215), Viṣṇumāyā (339), Kālarātri and others noted on the verses — and both texts treat the Goddess as the power behind Viṣṇu and Brahmā. These are shared Śākta ideas, not evidence that one text depends on the other; no specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine is stated in this chapter.

key_verses.why: Mahāmāyā deludes the world and draws even the wise into delusion.
She is the supreme knowledge, the eternal cause of liberation.
Eternal, the world her form: the definition of the Goddess in the frame story.
त्वं स्वाहा त्वं स्वधा — the opening of Brahmā’s hymn.
You are Sandhyā and Sāvitrī, the supreme mother; by you this universe is borne and created (continued in 1.76: protected, and consumed at the end).
Whatever thing exists anywhere, real or unreal — with 1.83: the power of all of it is you; how then can you be praised?

comm.t: The speaker label that opens the Devī Māhātmya. In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa the sage Mārkaṇḍeya is answering his pupil Krauṣṭuki’s questions about the ages of the Manus; the whole of the Devī Māhātmya is a story told inside that answer.

The Gita Press pāṭha counts every uvāca line as a mantra, which is how the text reaches seven hundred (the chapter colophons count them separately: 57 uvāca mantras in all). In recitation this first mantra carries the bījas ॐ ऐं, which belong to the pāṭha, not to the Purāṇa.

mantras.anvaya: यः सूर्यतनयः सावर्णिः अष्टमः मनुः कथ्यते, तदुत्पत्तिं विस्तरात् गदतः मम निशामय।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (यः … कथ्यते) names the subject; the main clause is the imperative निशामय with its object तदुत्पत्तिम्, and गदतः मम gives the speaker.
mantras.lit: Sāvarṇi, the son of the Sun, who is called the eighth Manu — hear his origin from me as I tell it in detail.
mantras.tr: Sāvarṇi, the Sun’s son, is spoken of as the eighth Manu. Listen as I tell you at length how he came to be.

comm.t: Mārkaṇḍeya announces his subject: the origin of Sāvarṇi, the eighth Manu. The frame closes in the last mantra of the text (13.29), where King Suratha is promised rebirth from the Sun as Sāvarṇi. The glory of the Goddess is told as the answer to a question about a Manu.
The chapter colophons place the text in the Purāṇa’s account of the Sāvarṇika manvantara (सावर्णिके मन्वन्तरे). Each Manu presides over one age of the world; the eighth age is still to come.
A modern reading: the Goddess first appears inside an ordinary story of loss and succession. Grace, in this text, works through history, not around it.

mantras.lit: How, by the power of Mahāmāyā, that greatly fortunate Sāvarṇi, son of Ravi, became lord of a manvantara —
mantras.tr: Hear how, by the grace of Mahāmāyā, that blessed Sāvarṇi, son of the Sun, came to rule an age of the world.
mantras.tr_note: The verse continues the sentence of 1.2; ‘Hear’ is supplied from निशामय there.

comm.t: The cause of Sāvarṇi’s rise is stated at once: the power (अनुभाव) of Mahāmāyā. The story of Suratha that follows (1.4 onward) explains how.

Mahāmāyā is the name under which the first carita knows the Goddess: the power that binds beings in attachment (1.55–58) and the power that releases them. The same name returns in Medhas’s teaching (1.55) and in Brahmā’s hymn.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also names her Mahāmāyā (name 215, महामाया). The shared name is a shared idea in Śākta thought; the two texts remain separate works.

mantras.lit: Formerly, in the Svārociṣa interval, there was over the whole circle of the earth a king named Suratha, born in Caitra’s line.
mantras.tr: Long ago, in the age of Svārociṣa Manu, there lived a king named Suratha, of the line of Caitra, who ruled the whole earth.

comm.t: Suratha is introduced: a universal king of an earlier age. The story will take everything from him, in order (1.5–9).

Suratha is the king who, at the end of the text, receives his kingdom back and is promised birth as Sāvarṇi (13.25–29). His companion, the merchant Samādhi, will ask for knowledge instead. The tradition reads the pair as the two goals the Goddess grants: enjoyment (bhoga) and liberation (mokṣa).

morph.note: Present participle of the curādi stem पालय- (+ śatṛ → पालयत्), genitive singular. With तस्य it gives the circumstance: ‘while he was ruling’. The genitive can be read simply as possessive (‘his enemies’) or as the genitive absolute of disregard (‘though he ruled well, kings became his enemies’); the narrative supports both.
Perfect of √भू, third person plural (-उः). With a predicate nominative, ‘became’: भूपाः शत्रवः बभूवुः ‘kings became (his) enemies’.

mantras.anvaya: प्रजाः औरसान् पुत्रान् इव सम्यक् पालयतः तस्य तदा कोलाविध्वंसिनः भूपाः शत्रवः बभूवुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The genitive phrase (तस्य पालयतः …) frames the clause; the subject is भूपाः with its epithet कोलाविध्वंसिनः, शत्रवः is the predicate, बभूवुः the verb.
mantras.lit: Of him, as he protected his subjects rightly like his own sons, the kings, the Kolāvidhvaṃsins, then became enemies.
mantras.tr: While he ruled his people justly, as though they were his own children, the kings called the Kolāvidhvaṃsins rose against him as enemies.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Rose against him’ renders बभूवुः शत्रवः (‘became enemies’) with the genitive तस्य.

comm.t: The first loss begins. Suratha is a good king — he rules his subjects ‘like his own sons’ — and still enemies arise. The text gives no fault on his side as the cause.
Ruling one’s people as one’s own children is the classical ideal of kingship in the epics and Purāṇas; the verse states it in a single simile and moves on.

flags.uncertain: कोलाविध्वंसिनः: whether a proper name of a people or dynasty or a description (‘destroyers of Kolā’), and what Kolā refers to (a city is often assumed), cannot be settled from the text.

samasa.sense: a king whose army and power of punishment were very great
samasa.alt: दण्ड can mean the army or the king’s power to punish (daṇḍanīti); both fit, and the contrast with न्यूनैः (‘weaker’) favours military strength.

morph.note: Past passive participle of √जि with the auxiliary ‘was’ understood: सः … जितः ‘he (was) defeated’. The agent is in the instrumental (कोलाविध्वंसिभिः).
Imperfect of √भू with augment a-: ‘(a battle) took place’. The narrative moves between imperfect, aorist and perfect without difference of sense.

mantras.anvaya: अतिप्रबलदण्डिनः तस्य तैः युद्धम् अभवत्। न्यूनैः अपि तैः कोलाविध्वंसिभिः सः युद्धे जितः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: a battle took place (युद्धम् अभवत्); he was defeated (सः जितः), with the agent and its concessive qualifier न्यूनैः अपि.
mantras.lit: A battle took place between him, who had a very strong force, and them; even though they were weaker, he was defeated in battle by those Kolāvidhvaṃsins.
mantras.tr: War broke out between them and the king, mighty as his forces were; and though they were the weaker side, the Kolāvidhvaṃsins defeated him in battle.

comm.t: The paradox is in अपि: the strong king loses to the weaker side. The verse does not explain it; the following verses show his own ministers turning against him.
A modern reading: strength on paper does not decide the outcome. The story strips Suratha of power that was never as secure as it looked.

mantras.anvaya: ततः स्वपुरम् आयातः (सः) निजदेशाधिपः अभवत्। तदा सः महाभागः तैः प्रबलारिभिः आक्रान्तः।
mantras.anvaya_en: First sentence: participle + predicate nominative + verb. Second: passive participle as verb with an instrumental agent.
mantras.lit: Then, having come to his own city, he became ruler of his own country; then that illustrious one was attacked by them, the powerful enemies.
mantras.tr: Then he withdrew to his own city and ruled only his own land; and even there that noble king was assailed by those enemies, now grown strong.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Only’ and ‘even there’ make explicit the contrast with 1.4 (‘over the whole earth’), which the compound निजदेशाधिपः implies.

comm.t: The second loss: the emperor of 1.4 is reduced to his home territory, and the enemies follow him there.
The steps of Suratha’s fall — empire, country, city, treasury, army — are told in order, so that by 1.9 nothing royal is left to him but the name महाभाग.

Instrumental plural of बलिन्, an -in stem (बल + possessive -in): ‘having strength’. Contrast दुर्बलस्य in the same line: the ministers are strong, the king weak.

mantras.anvaya: ततः तत्र स्वपुरे अपि बलिभिः दुष्टैः दुरात्मभिः अमात्यैः दुर्बलस्य (तस्य) कोशः बलं च अपहृतम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: The passive participle अपहृतम् is the verb; its subjects are कोशः बलं च, its agent the ministers with three adjectives, and दुर्बलस्य names whose treasury.
mantras.lit: Then, even there in his own city, the treasury and the army of the weakened one were carried off by his powerful, corrupt, evil-minded ministers.
mantras.tr: Then, in his own city too, his powerful ministers — corrupt and wicked men — seized the weakened king’s treasury and army.

comm.t: The third loss comes from inside: his own ministers take the treasury (कोश) and the army (बल), the two supports of kingship. The king is now called दुर्बल ‘weak’, the ministers बलिन् ‘strong’.
Treasury and army are two of the classical ‘limbs’ of the state (rājyāṅga); Suratha will speak of his attachment to the limbs of his kingdom in 1.41.

mantras.anvaya: ततः हृतस्वाम्यः सः भूपतिः मृगयाव्याजेन एकाकी हयम् आरुह्य गहनं वनं जगाम।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject with its bahuvrīhi epithet, the manner (मृगयाव्याजेन, एकाकी), the absolutive with its object, then the main verb with its goal.
mantras.lit: Then that king, robbed of his sovereignty, on the pretext of hunting, alone, having mounted a horse, went to a dense forest.
mantras.tr: Stripped of his kingdom, the king rode out alone on horseback under the pretext of a hunt, and went into a deep forest.

comm.t: The last step: the king leaves alone, keeping up appearances (‘as if to hunt’). The forest is where the story can turn.
A modern reading: the pretext matters. Even in defeat Suratha is guarding how he is seen — the attachment to position that he will confess in 1.12–16.

morph.note: s-aorist of √दृश्: augment अ-; the root takes an inserted a (दृश् → द्रश्), lengthened in this aorist (द्राश्); ś becomes k before the aorist s, which turns to ṣ (द्राक्ष्); ending -ईत्. The present uses the suppletive stem पश्य-; the aorist is built on the root itself.
Genitive singular of the s-stem मेधस्; the same form could be nominative/accusative plural of a different stem, but the sense here is ‘of Medhas’. The name means ‘intelligence, wisdom’.

mantras.anvaya: सः तत्र द्विजवर्यस्य मेधसः प्रशान्तश्वापदाकीर्णं मुनिशिष्योपशोभितम् आश्रमम् अद्राक्षीत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject, place, the owner of the hermitage (genitive), two compound adjectives of the object, the object, and the verb.
mantras.lit: There he saw the hermitage of Medhas, best of the twice-born, filled with beasts of prey grown peaceful and graced by the sage’s disciples.
mantras.tr: There he came upon the hermitage of Medhas, foremost of brahmins — a place where even the wild beasts had grown gentle, graced by the sage’s disciples.

comm.t: The turning point of the frame story. In the forest the king finds Medhas, who will become his teacher; the rest of the Devī Māhātmya is Medhas’s answer to his question (1.40 onward).
Predators living peacefully around a sage is a common sign, in epic and Purāṇic description, of the power of an ascetic’s calm. The setting shows what Suratha does not yet have.

mantras.lit: And he stayed for some time, honoured by that sage, wandering here and there in that hermitage of the excellent sage.
mantras.tr: Welcomed with honour by the sage, he stayed there for a while, wandering here and there about the great sage’s hermitage.

comm.t: Suratha is received as a guest and stays. He has not yet asked anything; his wandering ‘here and there’ prepares the restless thoughts of the next verses.
A modern reading: the body is at rest in a peaceful place, the mind is not. Outer refuge does not by itself settle inner turmoil.

morph.note: ममत्व is the genitive मम ‘of me’ made into an abstract noun with -त्व: ‘mine-ness’, possessiveness. The word returns in 1.41 and 1.44 (ममत्वाकृष्टमानसौ), where the king and the merchant both confess it.
Participle of √हा ‘to leave’ (हीन ‘left, lacking’). With an instrumental it means ‘deprived of’: मया हीनम् ‘deprived of me’.

mantras.anvaya: तदा तत्र ममत्वाकृष्टचेतनः सः अचिन्तयत् — पूर्वं मत्पूर्वैः पालितं मया हीनं तत् पुरं हि …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line introduces the king’s thought; the second line begins it (the thought runs to 1.16), with पुरम् the subject of पाल्यते in 1.13.
mantras.lit: Then, there, he, his mind drawn by possessiveness, thought: ‘That city, protected formerly by my forefathers, now deprived of me —
mantras.tr: Then, his mind still held by the sense of ‘mine’, he brooded: ‘That city my forefathers once protected, now bereft of me —
mantras.tr_note: ‘Now’ is supplied for the contrast with पूर्वम्; the sentence is completed in 1.13.

comm.t: The cause of Suratha’s grief is named at once: ममत्व, the feeling of ‘mine’. His thoughts (1.12–16) are a list of things he no longer owns — city, elephant, servants, treasury.

ममत्व is the theme of the frame story. At the end the merchant asks the Goddess for the knowledge that removes ‘mine’ and ‘I’ (13.18: ममेत्यहमिति … सङ्गविच्युतिकारकम्), while the king asks for his kingdom (13.17).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess as free of and destroying this very thing: names 164 निर्ममा and 165 ममताहन्त्री. The two texts are distinct; the shared idea is the possessiveness the Goddess removes.

Present ātmanepada first singular of √ज्ञा (kryādi): the weak stem जानी- loses its ī before a vowel ending, जान् + ए → जाने. न जाने ‘I do not know’ introduces the next worry, which runs into 1.14.

mantras.anvaya: (तत् पुरं) तैः असद्वृत्तैः मद्भृत्यैः धर्मतः पाल्यते न वा (इति) न जाने। सः मे प्रधानः सदामदः शूरहस्ती …
mantras.anvaya_en: न जाने governs the question पाल्यते न वा; the second line begins a new subject (the elephant), whose verbs are in 1.14.
mantras.lit: ‘— whether it is protected according to dharma by those servants of mine of bad conduct, or not, I do not know. That chief war-elephant of mine, always in rut —
mantras.tr: is it being ruled justly by those faithless servants of mine, or not? I cannot know. And my chief war-elephant, ever in rut —
mantras.tr_note: न जाने is attached to the first question in the literal version; the readable one lets it stand between the two worries, as the line does.

comm.t: Two worries: whether his city is ruled rightly, and what has become of his favourite elephant. The king still thinks as an owner — ‘my servants’, ‘my elephant’ (मे).
A modern reading: the grief is real but oddly specific. Loss often attaches itself to one cherished thing — here an elephant — that stands for the whole of what was taken.

mantras.anvaya: (सः शूरहस्ती) मम वैरिवशं यातः कान् भोगान् उपलप्स्यते? ये प्रसादधनभोजनैः नित्यं मम अनुगताः, (ते …)
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the elephant sentence of 1.13; the second opens a relative clause whose main clause (ते … कुर्वन्ति) is in 1.15.
mantras.lit: ‘— having gone into the power of my enemies, what enjoyments will it obtain? Those who always followed me, through favours, wealth and meals —
mantras.tr: now fallen into my enemies’ hands, what comforts will it find? And those who always followed me, won by my favour, my gifts and my table —

comm.t: The king pities his elephant, then turns to his retainers, who were bound to him by what he gave: favour, money and food. The next verse says where their loyalty has gone.
A modern reading: loyalty bought with favour, wealth and food follows the giver of those things, not the person. Suratha half sees this, and still grieves.

mantras.lit: ‘— they surely now render service to other kings. By those given to improper spending, constantly making expenditure —
mantras.tr: surely they now pay court to other kings. And by those wastrels, spending without pause —

comm.t: The king imagines his former followers serving his rivals, and his ministers squandering his treasury. Both thoughts are guesses; he has no news.
A modern reading: anxiety supplies certainties (ध्रुवम्, ‘surely’) that the mind has no way of checking. Suratha suffers over events he can only imagine.

mantras.anvaya: (तैः) अतिदुःखेन संचितः सः कोशः क्षयं गमिष्यति। एतत् च अन्यत् च पार्थिवः सततं चिन्तयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence begun in 1.15b (‘through them … the treasury will go to ruin’); the second closes the king’s thoughts (1.12–16) and is the narrator’s.
mantras.lit: ‘— that treasury, amassed with great hardship, will go to ruin.’ This and other things the king pondered constantly.
mantras.tr: the treasury I gathered with such toil will be drained away.’ These and other thoughts filled the king’s mind without rest.
mantras.tr_note: ‘I’ is supplied: the Sanskrit says only ‘amassed with great hardship’.

comm.t: The last of the king’s worries is the treasury; the narrator then closes the passage: he thought of ‘this and other things’ ceaselessly. No इति marks the end of the thought; the change of verb (चिन्तयामास) does.
Suratha’s monologue moves through city, elephant, retainers and treasury — the things of a kingdom. Medhas’s later teaching treats all of them as objects of ममत्व held in place by Mahāmāyā.

mantras.anvaya: तत्र विप्राश्रमाभ्याशे सः एकं वैश्यं ददर्श। सः तेन पृष्टः — भोः, त्वं कः? अत्र आगमने च हेतुः कः?
mantras.anvaya_en: Two narrative clauses (the king saw; the merchant was asked) and the direct question, which continues into 1.18.
mantras.lit: There, near the brahmin’s hermitage, he saw a certain merchant. He was asked by him: ‘Who are you, sir? And what is the reason for your coming here?
mantras.tr: There, near the sage’s hermitage, he saw a merchant, and asked him: ‘Who are you, friend? What has brought you here?
mantras.tr_note: The passive (‘he was asked by him’) is turned into an active sentence.

comm.t: The second figure of the frame story appears: a merchant, met by chance near the hermitage. The king, absorbed in his own losses until now, notices another man’s grief and speaks first.

The meeting of the deposed king and the disowned merchant pairs two kinds of loss — power and family. The tradition reads the two as the seekers of enjoyment and of liberation, as their final requests in chapter 13 show.

mantras.tr: Why do you look so sorrowful, so heavy-hearted?’ Hearing these kindly words of the king,

A modern reading: for the first time since 1.5 Suratha’s attention leaves his own losses. Concern for another’s sorrow opens the conversation that leads to the teaching.

morph.note: Participle of वि + √हा ‘to leave’: ‘left without, deprived of’, construed with the instrumental (धनैः दारैः पुत्रैः).

Absolutive of आ + √दा ‘to take’. Its logical subject is not the speaker but those who wronged him — the sons and wife (or the kinsmen of 1.23): ‘having taken my wealth, (they cast me out)’. Such a shift of subject is common in epic narrative.
दार ‘wife’ is masculine and used in the plural for a single wife — a fixed idiom.

mantras.anvaya: धनलोभात् असाधुभिः पुत्रदारैः (अहं) निरस्तः च, धनैः दारैः पुत्रैः च विहीनः; (ते) मे धनम् आदाय (1.23: आप्तबन्धुभिः च निरस्तः) …
mantras.anvaya_en: Two predicates of an implied अहम् (निरस्तः, विहीनः); the absolutive phrase आदाय मे धनम् belongs with the agents who cast him out and runs into 1.23.
mantras.lit: And I have been cast out by my wicked sons and wife out of greed for wealth, and am deprived of wealth, wife and sons; (they,) having taken my wealth —
mantras.tr: My wicked sons and wife, greedy for my wealth, have driven me out. I am left without money, wife or sons; they have taken all I had,
mantras.tr_note: ‘All I had’ renders मे धनम् ‘my wealth’; the subject ‘they’ of आदाय is supplied.

comm.t: The merchant’s answer to ‘why have you come?’: his own family has thrown him out to take his wealth. His loss mirrors the king’s — Suratha was betrayed by ministers, Samādhi by sons and wife.
Unlike the king, the merchant names his betrayers as his nearest kin; the point is made sharper in 1.31–34, where he confesses that his heart still goes out to them.

flags.uncertain: The construction of the second line admits two readings: (a) धनैः दारैः पुत्रैः all depend on विहीनः (‘deprived of wealth, wife and sons’), with आदाय मे धनम् referring to the relatives; (b) विहीनः धनैः only, with दारैः पुत्रैः as the agents of आदाय (‘deprived of wealth, my wife and sons having taken it’). Reading (a) is followed here as the more natural word order.

Active kta of a verb of motion with two prefixes, अभि + आ: ‘(I) have come’ (to the forest).
आत्मक ‘having the nature of, consisting of’ (आत्मन् + -क) makes its feminine in -इका: आत्मिका. It agrees with प्रवृत्तिम् (f.) in the next verse.

mantras.anvaya: (अहं) दुःखी आप्तबन्धुभिः च निरस्तः वनम् अभ्यागतः। सः अहम् अत्र संस्थितः पुत्राणां … कुशलाकुशलात्मिकां (प्रवृत्तिं) न वेद्मि (1.24)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line ends the account of his expulsion; the second begins a sentence completed in 1.24 (न वेद्मि … प्रवृत्तिम्).
mantras.lit: — and cast out by trusted kinsmen, I have come, sorrowful, to the forest. I, such as I am, do not know the (news), of good or ill, of my sons,
mantras.tr: and, cast off by the kinsmen I trusted, I have come to this forest in grief. Now I do not know whether things go well or ill with my sons,

comm.t: The merchant’s second answer: he came to the forest because his own people drove him out. Yet his first thought is not of his wrong but of their welfare, which he cannot learn.
A modern reading: he has been thrown out and robbed, and still worries whether those who did it are well. The text shows the bond outliving the betrayal before it names it as a puzzle (1.31–34).

mantras.anvaya: अत्र संस्थितः (अहं) पुत्राणां स्वजनानां च दाराणां च प्रवृत्तिं न वेद्मि (1.23)। तेषां गृहे साम्प्रतं क्षेमं किं नु, अक्षेमं किं नु?
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes न वेद्मि of 1.23 with its object; the second is a double question (किं नु … किं नु).
mantras.lit: — (the news) of my own people and of my wife, staying here. Is it, I wonder, welfare in their house, or ill-fare, at present?
mantras.tr: or with my kin and my wife, for I am here, far away. Is all well in their home now, or is it not?
mantras.tr_note: ‘Far away’ draws out अत्र संस्थितः (‘staying here’), which explains why he has no news.

comm.t: The sentence of 1.23 ends: he has no tidings of sons, kin or wife because he is here in the forest. He asks twice, with किं नु, whether they are well.

mantras.anvaya_en: A short question (कथं ते) and a double question with किं नु … किं नु.
mantras.lit: How are they? Are my sons, I wonder, of good conduct, or of bad conduct?
mantras.tr: How are they? Are my sons living rightly now, or have they gone astray?
mantras.tr_note: ‘Now’ is supplied from साम्प्रतम् in 1.24.

comm.t: The merchant ends his answer with anxious questions about the very sons who robbed him. The king will ask next (1.27–28) why he still cares for them.
A modern reading: he does not ask whether they regret what they did, only whether they are good. Attachment here takes the form of hope for those who caused the hurt.

morph.note: Past passive participle of निर् + √अस् ‘throw’: ‘thrown out’. With the instrumental यैः it makes a passive clause: ‘by whom you were cast out’.
The polite ‘you’: nominative of भवत्, a pronoun that takes the verb in the third person. Its final n meets the l of लुब्धैः and becomes a nasalised l (भवाँल्लुब्धैः).
Instrumental of cause: ‘because of (your) wealth’. The plural is idiomatic for ‘riches’. See Uncertain.

mantras.anvaya: यैः लुब्धैः पुत्रदारादिभिः धनैः (हेतुभिः) भवान् निरस्तः, (तेषु …)
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause only: its correlative तेषु and the main verb come in the next half-verse (1.28).
mantras.lit: Those greedy ones — sons, wife and the rest — by whom you were cast out on account of wealth,
mantras.tr: Those greedy ones — your sons, your wife and the rest — who drove you out for the sake of your wealth:
mantras.tr_note: The sentence is completed in 1.28.

comm.t: The king restates Samādhi’s own account (1.22: ‘cast out by sons and wife out of greed for wealth’). The question it leads to comes in the next half-verse.

Read with 1.12–14, the question is ironic: Suratha has just been worrying, in the same way, about the kingdom, servants and elephant that were taken from him. He asks the merchant what he cannot yet answer for himself; he admits as much in 1.41–45.

flags.uncertain: धनैः: the instrumental plural is read here as cause (‘on account of wealth’). Some translators take it loosely as ‘(deprived) of your wealth’, echoing 1.22 (पुत्रैरादाय मे धनम्). The reading itself is not in doubt.

comm.t: The king’s question: why love those who have wronged you? It is the question of the whole first carita, and the merchant will answer that he does not know (1.31–34).
A modern reading: the question is easier to ask of another than of oneself. The text lets the king hear his own trouble in a stranger’s voice before he can name it.

morph.note: Present of √कृ (stem करो- before the first-person ending -मि). In a question the present is deliberative: ‘what am I to do?’
Absolutive with ल्यप् (-य), the form used when the verb has a prefix (contrast त्यक्त्वा). Its subject is the agent of the main verb, here the kin (यैः).
Abstract noun in -ता (taddhita तल्) from निष्ठुर ‘hard’. मनः निष्ठुरतां न बध्नाति: ‘the mind does not take on hardness’ — the merchant cannot make himself stop caring.

mantras.anvaya: किं करोमि? मम मनः निष्ठुरतां न बध्नाति। यैः धनलुब्धैः पितृस्नेहं संत्यज्य (अहं) निराकृतः, …
mantras.anvaya_en: A question, then a statement; the second line opens a relative clause (यैः … निराकृतः) whose correlative तेषु and main clause come in 1.32.
mantras.lit: What am I to do? My mind does not take on hardness. Those greedy for wealth by whom, having cast off love for a father, I was spurned —
mantras.tr: What can I do? My heart will not grow hard. Those who, greedy for my wealth, threw off the love they owed their father and drove me out —
mantras.tr_note: ‘my’ with wealth and ‘their’ with father are supplied from the context; the sentence continues in 1.32.

comm.t: The merchant answers with a helpless question. He knows how he was treated and cannot stop loving: his mind refuses the hardness that reason would justify.

The verb बन्ध् ‘to bind’ is the word the text will use for saṃsāra itself (संसारबन्ध, 1.58). Here it is turned around: the mind will not bind itself to hardness, because it is already bound by affection.

The prefix अभि sharpens ‘know’ to ‘understand, recognise’: the merchant knows the facts (जानन्) but cannot see into them (न अभिजानामि).

mantras.anvaya: (यैः) पतिस्वजनहार्दं च (संत्यज्य अहं निराकृतः), तेषु एव मे मनः हार्दि (अस्ति)। महामते, जानन् अपि एतत् किं (इति) न अभिजानामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first half closes the relative sentence of 1.31: पतिस्वजनहार्दम् is a second object of संत्यज्य, and तेषु … हार्दि is the main clause. The second half is a new sentence: an indirect question (किम् एतत्) governed by न अभिजानामि.
mantras.lit: — and affection for husband and kinsman: toward those very ones my mind is loving. What this is I do not understand, though knowing, O great-minded one.
mantras.tr: who threw off all feeling for husband and kinsman — toward them, still, my heart is full of love. I know all this, wise king, and yet I cannot understand it.

comm.t: The merchant states the paradox the sage will be asked to explain: he knows (जानन्) and yet does not understand (न अभिजानामि). The facts are clear to him; his heart does not follow them.
This is the condition Medhas will name in 1.55: Mahāmāyā draws away the minds even of those who know (ज्ञानिनामपि चेतांसि). Knowledge of the facts is not freedom from delusion.
A modern reading: the text separates information from understanding. The merchant is not ignorant; he is attached — and he is honest enough to say that the two are different.

mantras.anvaya_en: A यत् clause (‘that …’) spelling out the एतत् of 1.32: two statements, the first nominal (verb ‘is’ understood), the second with जायते.
mantras.lit: — that the mind is inclined to love even toward worthless kinsfolk; that on their account sighing and dejection arise in me.
mantras.tr: — that my heart leans in love toward kinsfolk who have shown no virtue, and that I sigh and grieve for their sake.
mantras.tr_note: ‘my’ with heart is supplied from मे in the second line; the verse explains the ‘this’ (एतत्) of 1.32.

comm.t: The merchant names what he cannot understand: love that persists toward the unworthy, and the sighing and gloom it brings. The symptoms are bodily (निःश्वास) and mental (दौर्मनस्य).

A modern reading: the verse does not call the love wrong. It reports, without judgement, that love does not wait for its object to deserve it — which is both the merchant’s pain and, later in the text, the shape of the Goddess’s own compassion.

comm.t: The two exiles are named side by side and come before the sage in due form. The courtesies are not skipped: the teaching that follows begins with the proper approach of the pupil.
A modern reading: the merchant’s name, Samādhi, is the word for meditative absorption. The text does not comment on it, but at its end (13.15ff) it is he who asks for knowledge rather than a kingdom.

comm.t: The king formally asks to put a question. After the approach (1.36–38) comes the request, and then the question itself (1.41–45).

The shape is that of a classical teaching dialogue: a pupil who has come with due courtesy asks one question, and the teacher’s answer becomes the text. The rest of the Devī Māhātmya unfolds as Medhas’s answer.

mantras.anvaya: यत् गतराज्यस्य मे अखिलेषु अपि राज्याङ्गेषु ममत्वं (अस्ति), (मम) मनसः दुःखाय, स्वचित्तायत्ततां विना, …
mantras.anvaya_en: A यत् clause (‘that …’), nominal, with ‘is’ understood; its subject is ममत्वम्. It is taken up by किम् एतत् in 1.42.
mantras.lit: That — to the grief of my mind, without (its) being under the control of my own mind — there is in me, whose kingdom is gone, a sense of ‘mine’ even toward all the limbs of the kingdom,
mantras.tr: My kingdom is gone, yet I still feel that every part of it is mine — against my own will, and to my mind’s distress,
mantras.tr_note: The Sanskrit is a ‘that …’ clause completed by ‘what is this?’ in 1.42; the translation makes it a statement. ‘Against my own will’ renders स्वचित्तायत्ततां विना.

comm.t: Now the king speaks of himself. He asked the merchant why he still loved those who had wronged him (1.27–28); here he admits the same bondage: he has lost his kingdom and cannot stop feeling it is his.

‘Limbs of the kingdom’ is a term of Indian political thought, where a state has seven limbs: the king, ministers, territory, fort, treasury, army and ally. The king’s earlier worries (1.12–14) touch several of them: his city, his servants, his elephant, his treasury.

mantras.tr: and deserted by his kin; yet he loves them dearly. So he and I alike are both in deep distress,

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the description of the two (from 1.43); the second asks the question proper, with a यत् clause explaining एतत्.
mantras.lit: — our minds dragged by possessiveness toward an object even though its fault has been seen. So what is this, O blessed one, that there is delusion even in (us) two who know?
mantras.tr: our minds dragged by the sense of ‘mine’ toward things whose faults we have plainly seen. Then what is this, blessed one — that even we, who know, are deluded?

comm.t: The question of the first carita, in its full form: why does delusion (मोह) persist in those who know? The king and the merchant both see the fault in what they cling to, and cling still.
The sage’s answer turns on two words of this verse. He takes up विषय at once (1.47–48), and he names the source of the मोह of ‘even those who know’ as Mahāmāyā (1.55, ज्ञानिनामपि चेतांसि).

comm.t: The king’s question ends. He distinguishes two things: they have knowledge (ज्ञान, 1.44) but lack discernment (विवेक), and so they are bewildered. The sage begins his answer in 1.47.

A modern reading: the king’s diagnosis is precise. Information is not the problem; the faculty that weighs it and lets go is. The rest of the chapter traces that failure to a power larger than the two men.

mantras.lit: And the sense-object, O blessed one, reaches (creatures) thus, severally. Some creatures are blind by day; likewise others are blind at night.
mantras.tr: And the world of objects, blessed one, reaches each creature in its own way. Some creatures are blind by day, others blind by night,
mantras.tr_note: ‘creatures’ in the first sentence is supplied; the Sanskrit says only that the object ‘goes’ severally.

comm.t: Medhas illustrates: knowledge of objects is not uniform. What a creature can know depends on its nature — some see only by night, some only by day. The text names no species.
The point prepares the next step: if knowing objects were what made a being wise, the animals would be wise too (1.49–50). The knowledge the king has is real but of this ordinary kind.

mantras.lit: And what is men’s is theirs; and the rest is likewise equal for both. Even though there is knowledge, look at these birds — into the beaks of their young
mantras.tr: and what men have, they have; in all else, too, the two are alike. Yet, for all their knowledge, look at these birds — into the beaks of their young
mantras.tr_note: The sentence runs on into 1.52: the birds are intent on dropping grain into those beaks.

comm.t: Medhas closes the comparison (humans and animals are alike in knowledge and in the rest) and points to an example. The demonstrative एतान् with the imperative पश्य suggests birds within sight at the hermitage.
The text does not say what ‘the rest’ (अन्यत्) is; the point is only that, in the ordinary life of the senses, humans and animals are on one level.

Ablative of cause: the birds act ‘from delusion’, not from calculation — the contrast with लोभात् (‘from greed’) in 1.53.
As a postposition (karmapravacanīya) प्रति takes the accusative: सुतान् प्रति ‘toward (their) sons’.

mantras.anvaya: (पतङ्गान्) मोहात् कणमोक्षादृतान्, क्षुधा पीड्यमानान् अपि (पश्य)। (हे) मनुजव्याघ्र, मानुषाः सुतान् प्रति साभिलाषाः (भवन्ति), …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the description of the birds (objects of पश्य in 1.51). The second begins a new statement about humans; its cause comes in 1.53.
mantras.lit: — intent, out of delusion, on letting fall grains, though tormented by hunger. Human beings, O tiger among men, are full of longing toward their sons
mantras.tr: they drop grain into them out of sheer delusion, though racked by hunger themselves. Men, tiger among men, long for sons
mantras.tr_note: ‘themselves’ makes plain that the hunger is the parent birds’ own. The second line runs on into 1.53.

comm.t: The birds feed their young while starving themselves, and the sage calls the motive मोह, delusion. Then he turns to humans, who also long for their children.

The two cases are not the same: the birds act from blind delusion, humans (1.53) from greed for a return. Both are forms of the attachment the king asked about, and both, Medhas says next, are the work of Mahāmāyā (1.54).

samasa.sense: caught in the circling pull of possessiveness
samasa.alt: Also read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, ममतायाः आवर्त्तः ‘the whirlpool of mine-ness’; the metaphorical reading fits the paired image मोहगर्ते.

samasa.literal: in the pit that is delusion
samasa.sense: fallen into bewilderment as into a pit
samasa.alt: Also ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, मोहस्य गर्तः; as above.

morph.note: Past passive participle of the causative of नि + √पत्: ‘made to fall, thrown down’. The causer is named in the next verse: by the power of Mahāmāyā (1.54).

ममता (मम + -ता) is the same idea as ममत्व in 1.41 and 1.44. आवर्त्त ‘whirlpool’ (आ + √वृत् ‘to turn’) is printed with a doubled t after r, a spelling the grammarians permit; it is the same word as आवर्त.
प्रत्युपकार ‘a service in return’ (प्रति + उपकार); the dative gives the purpose: parents cherish children ‘for the sake of a return’.

mantras.anvaya: (मानुषाः) लोभात् प्रत्युपकाराय (सुतान् प्रति साभिलाषाः)। ननु एतान् किं न पश्यसि? तथा अपि (एते) ममतावर्त्ते मोहगर्ते निपातिताः (महामायाप्रभावेण, 1.54)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first half finishes 1.52 (why men long for sons) and asks a rhetorical question. The second begins the sentence completed in 1.54: the beings are thrown into mamatā and moha by the power of Mahāmāyā.
mantras.lit: — out of greed, for a return of the favour. Surely you see these? Even so, (they are) cast down into the whirlpool of mine-ness, into the pit of delusion,
mantras.tr: out of greed, hoping to be repaid. Do you not see them? And still they are thrown into the whirlpool of ‘mine’, into the pit of delusion —
mantras.tr_note: The sentence is completed in 1.54: ‘by the power of Mahāmāyā, who keeps the world of saṃsāra in being’.

comm.t: Human love for children is mixed with self-interest: greed for a return. Yet humans and birds alike, knowing as they are, are thrown into the same whirlpool of possessiveness and pit of delusion. The next verse names who throws them.

The two images answer the king’s words: his ममत्व (1.41, 1.44) and मोह (1.44) return as the whirlpool and the pit. The sage’s answer is that this is not a private failure of the king and the merchant but the working of Mahāmāyā (1.54–56), who is also the cause of release (1.57).

The Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess from the other side of the same pair: ममताहन्त्री (165), ‘destroyer of mine-ness’, and मोहनाशिनी (163), ‘remover of delusion’. Here in the Devī Māhātmya the same power that casts beings into mamatā and moha is the one that frees them when she is gracious (1.57).

samasa.alt: Also read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, योगस्य निद्रा, ‘the sleep of yoga’; the sense is the same.

samasa.sense: of Viṣṇu (named as Hari in 1.55)

morph.note: Gerundive of √कृ with ṇyat: कृ + य → कार्य (vṛddhi of the root vowel). With न it expresses what ought not to be: विस्मयः न कार्यः ‘wonder is not to be made’ = ‘do not wonder’.
Instrumental singular of an -in stem: कारिन् + आ → कारिणा (n → ṇ after r). It agrees with प्रभावेण, not with महामाया: it is the power that keeps saṃsāra in place.

mantras.anvaya: (ते) संसारस्थितिकारिणा महामायाप्रभावेण (ममतावर्ते मोहगर्ते निपातिताः)। तत् अत्र विस्मयः न कार्यः। (एषा) जगत्पतेः योगनिद्रा …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence of 1.53 (‘they are thrown into the whirlpool of mine-ness … by the power of Mahāmāyā’). Then a short main clause with a gerundive (विस्मयः न कार्यः), and the opening of a new sentence that 1.55 completes (योगनिद्रा जगत्पतेः … एषा).
mantras.lit: (They are thrown down) by the power of Mahāmāyā, which makes the continuance of saṃsāra. Therefore no wonder is to be felt in this: the yogic sleep of the lord of the world —
mantras.tr: It is the power of Mahāmāyā, who keeps the round of worldly existence turning, that casts them down. So there is nothing to wonder at here. She who is the yogic sleep of the Lord of the world —
mantras.tr_note: The first line ends the sentence of 1.53; the last words begin the sentence completed in 1.55.

comm.t: The sage Medhas answers the king’s question (1.44–45: why are we attached when we see the fault?). Creatures who know better are still bound to their own, as the birds feeding their young show (1.51–53); the cause is the power of Mahāmāyā, so it is no cause for surprise. In the digital text a footnote asterisk of the printed book followed संसारस्थितिकारिणा; it has been removed (corrections.json, encoding).

The answer turns a psychological question into a theological one: attachment is not merely a private failure but the working of the power that keeps the world in being. The same Goddess is introduced in the same breath as Viṣṇu’s Yoganidrā, the name under which Brahmā will praise her (1.69–71).

samasa.alt: As a name it can also be taken as a bahuvrīhi, महती माया यस्याः सा ‘she whose māyā is great’; the karmadhāraya fits the identification with Yoganidrā better.

morph.note: Passive of a causative: मोहय- loses its causative -ay- before the passive -ya- (मोह् + य + ते). The world is the subject; तया names the agent: ‘the world is deluded by her’.
Neuter plural of चेतस्: the s-stems insert a nasal and lengthen the vowel in the nominative and accusative plural (चेतांसि, like मनांसि). Here accusative, looking forward to the verbs of 1.56.

mantras.anvaya: (या) जगत्पतेः योगनिद्रा, एषा हरेः महामाया च; तया जगत् सम्मोह्यते। सा हि भगवती देवी ज्ञानिनाम् अपि चेतांसि (बलात् आकृष्य मोहाय प्रयच्छति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line identifies the Yoganidrā of 1.54 with Hari’s Mahāmāyā and states her work with a passive (तया सम्मोह्यते जगत्). The second line begins a sentence completed in 1.56: चेतांसि is the object of आकृष्य … प्रयच्छति there, and देवी भगवती हि सा is a parenthesis giving the reason.
mantras.lit: — and this one is the Mahāmāyā of Hari; by her the world is deluded. The minds even of the wise — for she is the Goddess, the Blessed One —
mantras.tr: — she is Hari’s Great Māyā, and by her the whole world is held in delusion. Even the minds of the wise — for she is the Goddess, the Blessed Lady —
mantras.tr_note: The sentence is carried over from 1.54 and into 1.56, where the verbs governing चेतांसि stand.

comm.t: Medhas names the power: Viṣṇu’s Yoganidrā is the same as Hari’s Mahāmāyā, and the whole world is deluded by her. Even the wise are not exempt — the very point the king and the merchant found puzzling about themselves (1.44).

The verse joins two roles that the chapter keeps together: the sleep that holds Viṣṇu (the story of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, 1.66 onward) and the delusion that holds all beings. In the Śākta reading the god who sustains the world is himself subject to her, which is why his waking depends on her withdrawal (1.86–89).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has both names: 215, महामाया, and 339, विष्णुमाया. The Devī Māhātmya itself will later praise her as Viṣṇumāyā in the hymn of chapter 5; the two works remain distinct.

samasa.alt: Inside the dvandva, अचर is a nañ tatpuruṣa (न चरम्). Some take चराचर as an itaretara dvandva (चराः च अचराः च); as an adjective of the neuter singular जगत् the samāhāra form fits.

morph.note: √दा in the sense ‘give’ (दाण्) takes the stem यच्छ- in the present system: प्र-यच्छ-ति. With the dative मोहाय: ‘hands (them) over to delusion’.
Absolutive with a prefix takes -य (lyap) instead of -त्वा: आ-कृष्-य ‘having dragged’. Its subject is the subject of the main verb, Mahāmāyā.
Passive present of वि + √सृज्: ‘is emitted’, the Purāṇic word for creation as outflow (visarga).

mantras.anvaya: (सा) महामाया ज्ञानिनाम् अपि चेतांसि बलात् आकृष्य मोहाय प्रयच्छति। तया एतत् विश्वं चराचरं जगत् विसृज्यते।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence begun in 1.55 (object चेतांसि); the second is a passive sentence with तया as agent.
mantras.lit: having dragged (them) by force, Mahāmāyā hands (them) over to delusion. By her is emitted this entire world, moving and unmoving.
mantras.tr: — Mahāmāyā seizes them by force and gives them over to delusion. It is she who brings forth this whole world of the moving and the still.

comm.t: Two works of the one Goddess are named: she forcibly binds even the wise in delusion, and she emits the entire world. Delusion and creation are put side by side as acts of the same power.

The force (बलात्) is stressed: knowledge alone does not free a person from attachment, which is why the next verse turns to her grace (प्रसन्ना). The tradition reads the sequence 1.55–58 as the theological core of Medhas’s teaching, to which the three caritas are the illustration.

mantras.anvaya: सा एषा प्रसन्ना (सती) नृणां मुक्तये वरदा भवति। सा परमा विद्या, सनातनी, मुक्तेः हेतुभूता (च)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: a verbal one (सा … वरदा भवति) with a dative of purpose, and a nominal one (सा विद्या परमा … हेतुभूता सनातनी) that 1.58 continues.
mantras.lit: She, this one, when pleased, becomes boon-giving to men for liberation. She is the supreme knowledge, the eternal cause of liberation,
mantras.tr: And when she is pleased, this same Goddess grants human beings the boon of liberation. She is the supreme knowledge, the eternal cause of freedom —

comm.t: The power that binds (1.55–56) is the same power that frees. When she is gracious she grants liberation; as supreme knowledge she is its eternal cause.

The Śākta tradition reads this verse with 1.58 as the key to the text: bondage and release both come from her, so release is sought by turning to her, not by escaping her. The rest of the Devī Māhātmya — and Suratha’s and Samādhi’s boons in chapter 13 — is the working out of प्रसन्ना वरदा.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names her 402, विद्याऽविद्यास्वरूपिणी, ‘whose form is both knowledge and ignorance’, and 331, वरदा. The pairing of binding and freeing in one Goddess is common Śākta ground; the texts are separate.

samasa.sense: sovereign even over the gods who rule the world
samasa.alt: Or सर्वस्य ईश्वरः सर्वेश्वरः (the Lord of all, i.e. Viṣṇu or Śiva), तस्य ईश्वरी ‘ruler of the Lord of all’. Either way she stands above the highest god — which fits a verse spoken of Viṣṇu’s Yoganidrā.

morph.note: A feminine subject with a masculine predicate noun: हेतु is a masculine noun and does not change gender to agree, as in English ‘she is the cause’.

mantras.anvaya: सा एव संसारबन्धहेतुः च, सर्वेश्वरेश्वरी (च)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A nominal sentence continuing 1.57: सा (subject) with two predicates.
mantras.lit: and the cause of the bondage of saṃsāra; she alone is the sovereign of the sovereigns of all.
mantras.tr: and the cause of bondage to worldly existence. She alone is sovereign over all who rule.

comm.t: The teaching closes on its paradox: the cause of liberation (1.57) is also the cause of bondage, and she alone (सैव) is both. She is therefore above every ruling power, including the gods.
With this half-verse Medhas’s answer to the king is complete, and the king’s next question (1.60–62) follows from it: who is this Goddess? The three caritas are told as the answer.

A modern reading: what holds us and what frees us may not be two different things. The same capacity for attachment that binds a parent to a child (the birds of 1.51–52) is, turned rightly, the capacity for devotion.

mantras.anvaya: भगवन्, यां भवान् महामाया इति (ब्रवीति), सा देवी का हि?
mantras.anvaya_en: A direct question (का हि सा देवी) with a relative clause (यां भवान् … ब्रवीति) whose verb stands at the start of 1.61.
mantras.lit: O blessed one, who indeed is that Goddess whom your honour (calls) ‘Mahāmāyā’ —
mantras.tr: Revered sir, who is this Goddess whom you call Mahāmāyā?
mantras.tr_note: The verb of the relative clause, ब्रवीति, stands at the beginning of 1.61; the readable translation draws it back.

comm.t: The king takes up the name the sage used (1.55–56) and asks who she is. The question is the hinge of the whole text: everything that follows, through chapter 13, is Medhas’s answer.

Suratha’s questions in 1.60–62 — who she is, how she arose, what she does, her power, her nature, her origin — are traditionally read as the plan of the Devī Māhātmya: the three caritas show her arising and her deeds, and the hymns show her nature.

mantras.anvaya: (यां भवान् महामाया इति) ब्रवीति। द्विज, सा कथम् उत्पन्ना? अस्याः कर्म च किम्? सा देवी यत्प्रभावा, यत्स्वरूपा, यदुद्भवा च, …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first word completes the relative clause of 1.60. Two direct questions follow (कथम् … किम्), then three indirect questions in compound form, resumed by तत्सर्वम् in 1.62.
mantras.lit: — calls (Mahāmāyā): how did she arise, and what is her deed, O twice-born? And of what power that Goddess is, of what nature, of what origin —
mantras.tr: How did she come to be, O brāhmaṇa, and what are her deeds? What is her power, what her true nature, and from where does she arise?
mantras.tr_note: कर्म is singular (‘deed’); the readable version renders it as the collective ‘deeds’.

comm.t: The king asks six things: how she arose, what she does, her power, her nature, her origin — and, in 1.62, he asks to hear it all. He addresses Medhas as द्विज, a brāhmaṇa.

The sage’s answer (1.64–66) qualifies the first question at once: she is eternal, and is said to ‘arise’ only when she becomes manifest for the gods’ work. The questions about power and nature are answered less by definition than by the stories and the hymns.

comm.t: The king’s request closes: he wants to hear all of it from the sage, whom he honours as the best of Brahman-knowers. Medhas begins his answer at once (1.63).

mantras.anvaya: सा नित्या एव, जगन्मूर्तिः; तया इदं सर्वं ततम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two nominal sentences: a description of her (नित्या एव … जगन्मूर्तिः) and a passive statement with a participle as predicate (तया … ततम्).
mantras.lit: She is eternal indeed, having the world as her form; by her all this is pervaded.
mantras.tr: She is eternal; the world is her very form, and by her all this is pervaded.

comm.t: The sage’s first answer corrects the king’s first question (‘how did she arise?’, 1.61): she is eternal and has no birth. The world is her form, and all of it is filled by her.

The phrase तया सर्वमिदं ततम् echoes the Bhagavad Gītā’s language for the pervading Absolute (येन सर्वमिदं ततम्, 2.17; मया ततमिदं सर्वम्, 9.4). The Devī Māhātmya applies to the Goddess what the Gītā says of the imperishable and of Kṛṣṇa.

mantras.anvaya: तथा अपि मम (मत्तः) तत्समुत्पत्तिः बहुधा श्रूयताम्। यदा सा देवानां कार्यसिद्ध्यर्थम् आविर्भवति, (तदा …)
mantras.anvaya_en: A passive imperative sentence, then a यदा clause whose main clause (तदा …) is in 1.66.
mantras.lit: Even so, let her arising, in many ways, be heard from me. When she becomes manifest for the accomplishment of the purpose of the gods —
mantras.tr: Even so, hear from me how she comes forth, again and again. When she becomes manifest to accomplish the purpose of the gods,

comm.t: Although she is eternal, she has many ‘arisings’, and the sage will tell them. Each is a manifestation (आविर्भाव) for the gods’ need — the pattern of all three caritas.

The three caritas — the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, of Mahiṣa, and of Śumbha and Niśumbha — are traditionally read as three such manifestations. The Gita Press pāṭha assigns them the presiding forms Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī; that assignment is liturgical tradition, not stated in this verse.

mantras.anvaya: (यदा सा … आविर्भवति,) तदा सा नित्या अपि लोके उत्पन्ना इति अभिधीयते। (कल्पान्ते) जगति एकार्णवीकृते यदा विष्णुः योगनिद्राम् (अभजत्), …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is the main clause answering यदा in 1.65 (तदा … अभिधीयते). The second line opens a new यदा clause whose verb अभजत् and main clause (तदा …) are in 1.67.
mantras.lit: — then in the world she, though eternal, is called ‘born’. When Viṣṇu, the world having been made one ocean, (resorted to) Yoganidrā —
mantras.tr: then, though eternal, she is said in the world to be ‘born’. At the end of an age, when the world had become a single ocean and Viṣṇu entered his yogic sleep,
mantras.tr_note: ‘At the end of an age’ is drawn from कल्पान्ते in 1.67, and ‘entered’ renders अभजत् there.

comm.t: The answer to ‘how did she arise?’ is completed: her ‘birth’ is a way of speaking about her appearing. The second line begins the first story, set at the dissolution, when the world is one ocean and Viṣṇu lies in yogic sleep.

The distinction between eternal being and occasional manifestation governs the whole text: the Goddess of the three caritas is not three goddesses but one, appearing as the need arises. The idea runs parallel to Bhagavad Gītā 4.6–8 (अजोऽपि सन्नव्ययात्मा …), where the Lord, though unborn, comes into being from age to age for the protection of the good.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line ends the यदा clause begun in 1.66; the second begins the main clause (तदा …), whose predicate उद्यतौ is in 1.68.
mantras.lit: — having spread out Śeṣa, the Blessed Lord resorted (to it) at the end of the kalpa; then two terrible asuras, the renowned Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
mantras.tr: spreading out the serpent Śeṣa as his couch — then two dreadful asuras, the notorious Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
mantras.tr_note: The readable version keeps the verse’s order across 1.66–68; ‘the Blessed Lord’ and ‘at the end of the kalpa’ are rendered in 1.66’s readable line.

comm.t: The scene is set: at the dissolution, Viṣṇu lies on the serpent Śeṣa in yogic sleep on the single ocean. Two asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, appear.

Śeṣa (‘the remainder’) is the serpent who remains when all else is dissolved. The first carita is traditionally presided over by Mahākālī in the Gita Press pāṭha; that is liturgical tradition, not stated in the text.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the main clause of 1.67. The second introduces the subject (सः … ब्रह्मा प्रजापतिः) of a sentence whose verb, तुष्टाव, is in 1.69.
mantras.lit: — sprung from the wax of Viṣṇu’s ears, were intent on killing Brahmā. He, Brahmā, the lord of creatures, stationed on the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu,
mantras.tr: born from the wax of Viṣṇu’s ears, rose up to kill Brahmā. Brahmā, lord of creatures, seated on the lotus springing from Viṣṇu’s navel,

comm.t: The asuras are born from the sleeping Viṣṇu’s own ear-wax and set out to kill Brahmā, who sits on the lotus from Viṣṇu’s navel. The creator is threatened by what comes from the sustainer while the sustainer sleeps.
The tradition reads the image closely: danger arises from Viṣṇu himself while he is held by Yoganidrā, and Brahmā cannot wake him directly. He must turn to the power that holds Viṣṇu — the Goddess.
A modern reading: what threatens creation is born of the sleeper’s own neglect. The remedy the story offers is not force but praise — attention turned to the power at work.

mantras.anvaya: (सः ब्रह्मा) तौ उग्रौ असुरौ च प्रसुप्तं जनार्दनं च दृष्ट्वा एकाग्रहृदयस्थितः तां योगनिद्रां तुष्टाव।
mantras.anvaya_en: The subject (ब्रह्मा) comes from 1.68; an absolutive phrase with two objects joined by च … च, then the main verb with its object.
mantras.lit: having seen both those two fierce asuras and Janārdana fast asleep, praised that Yoganidrā, steadied in a one-pointed heart —
mantras.tr: seeing the two fierce asuras and Janārdana deep in sleep, with his heart wholly gathered, began to praise Yoganidrā —

comm.t: Brahmā sees the danger and sees that Viṣṇu cannot help while asleep. With a one-pointed heart he praises Yoganidrā, the power holding Viṣṇu — the hymn of 1.73–87.
The narrative logic is precise: to wake Viṣṇu, Brahmā addresses not Viṣṇu but the sleep that holds him. In the Śākta reading even the highest god’s activity depends on her release.

mantras.anvaya: (ब्रह्मा) हरेः विबोधनार्थाय हरिनेत्रकृतालयां विश्वेश्वरीं जगद्धात्रीं स्थितिसंहारकारिणीं (तां योगनिद्रां तुष्टाव)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A string of accusative epithets in apposition to योगनिद्राम् (1.69), with a dative of purpose; the verb is तुष्टाव (1.69).
mantras.lit: for the sake of the awakening of Hari — (her) who had made her abode in Hari’s eyes, the sovereign of the universe, the supporter of the world, the maker of maintenance and dissolution,
mantras.tr: to wake Hari: she who dwelt in Hari’s eyes, sovereign of the universe, sustainer of the world, who preserves it and dissolves it —

comm.t: The purpose of Brahmā’s praise is stated — to wake Hari — and the Goddess is described by her place (resting in Viṣṇu’s eyes, as sleep) and her cosmic functions: sovereign, supporter, preserver and dissolver of the world.
The epithets already give her the works usually divided among the gods: preservation (Viṣṇu’s) and dissolution (Rudra’s). The hymn will add creation (1.75–77), so that all three belong to her.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same epithet, name 935, जगद्धात्री, and lists the three functions as separate names: 264, सृष्टिकर्त्री; 266, गोप्त्री; 268, संहारिणी.

mantras.tr_note: ‘Brahmā’ and ‘praised her’ are supplied from 1.68–69 to close the sentence.

comm.t: The last epithets: she is Viṣṇu’s Sleep, the Blessed One, beyond compare. The nominative प्रभुः restates the subject, Brahmā, before the hymn begins.
The Goddess is named here by her plainest name, निद्रा ‘sleep’, with the honorific भगवती: what holds the highest god is not a lesser power but the Blessed One herself.

flags.uncertain: The construction of तेजसः is open. Taken here with प्रभुः, ‘the lord of radiance’, an epithet of Brahmā (the subject); it can also be read with अतुलाम्, ‘(her) unequalled in radiance’, with प्रभुः simply ‘the Lord’. Both are grammatical; the sense of the verse is not affected.

mantras.anvaya_en: Three identity statements with त्वम् repeated; स्वरात्मिका qualifies the subject.
mantras.lit: You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, you indeed are the vaṣaṭ-call, you whose self is sound.
mantras.tr: You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā; you are the sacred cry Vaṣaṭ — your very self is the sound of the Veda.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Of the Veda’ interprets स्वर (see Samāsa).

comm.t: Brahmā opens by identifying the Goddess with the three ritual calls of Vedic sacrifice: svāhā (offering to the gods), svadhā (offering to the ancestors) and vaṣaṭ (the hotṛ’s call at the oblation). She is the very sound through which offering reaches its recipient.

The hymn begins with sacrificial speech because in the Vedic view the sacrifice sustains the world. To call her svāhā and svadhā is to make her the power by which gods and ancestors are fed — the support of both worlds. In Purāṇic myth Svāhā and Svadhā are also personified as goddesses, consorts of Agni and of the ancestors.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same pair as consecutive names: 535, स्वाहा, and 536, स्वधा.

samasa.alt: The printed text joins अर्धमात्रास्थिता; it can also be divided as two words, अर्धमात्रा स्थिता ‘(you) abide as the half-mora’, and then या refers to the half-mora. The compound is kept as printed.

samasa.sense: beyond articulation

morph.note: Gerundive of the causative of उद् + √चर् (उच्चारयति ‘pronounces’): उच्चार्य ‘to be pronounced’; with the negative अन्- ‘not pronounceable’.

Ambiguous form: n. loc. sg. of अक्षर (‘in the imperishable syllable’) or f. voc. sg. of अक्षरा (‘O Imperishable!’). The locative is chosen because it gives स्थिता its place and matches the half-mora of the next line.
The suffix -धा makes adverbs of manner from numerals: त्रिधा ‘in three ways’, बहुधा ‘in many ways’ (1.65).

mantras.anvaya: त्वं सुधा। त्वं नित्ये अक्षरे त्रिधा मात्रात्मिका स्थिता। (त्वं) या विशेषतः अनुच्चार्या, नित्या, अर्धमात्रास्थिता (असि)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A short identity (सुधा त्वम्), a participial predicate with a locative of place, and a second predicate expanded by a relative clause (या … विशेषतः).
mantras.lit: You are nectar; in the eternal imperishable (syllable) you abide threefold, having the morae as your self; you abide in the half-mora, eternal, (you) who cannot be uttered distinctly.
mantras.tr: You are the nectar of immortality. In the eternal, imperishable syllable you dwell as its three sounds; and you dwell in the half-measure beyond them, eternal, which no voice can utter as a separate sound.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Syllable’ and ‘its three sounds’ interpret अक्षर and मात्रा as the syllable Om and its parts a, u, m, the standard sense in this context.

comm.t: The Goddess is identified with the sacred syllable: she abides in its three morae (a, u, m) and in the half-mora — the fading resonance after m — which cannot be pronounced as a distinct sound. She is also सुधा, the nectar of immortality.

The analysis of Om into three measures and a fourth beyond utterance is Upaniṣadic: the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad treats a, u and m as the three states of waking, dream and deep sleep and the ‘measureless fourth’ (अमात्रः चतुर्थः) as the self beyond them. Brahmā places the Goddess both in the three and in what lies beyond them.

A modern reading: the hymn begins with words that can be spoken — svāhā, svadhā, vaṣaṭ — and moves at once to the part of the sacred sound that cannot be spoken. Praise here is a way of approaching what speech cannot hold.

flags.uncertain: अक्षरे नित्ये may be locative (‘in the eternal imperishable [syllable]’, chosen here) or two feminine vocatives (‘O Imperishable, O Eternal One’); both are grammatical and both are found in translations. अर्धमात्रास्थिता is printed as one word; a division into अर्धमात्रा स्थिता is equally possible.

mantras.anvaya_en: Identity statements (त्वम् … संध्या सावित्री; त्वम् … जननी परा), then two parallel passive sentences with त्वया as agent.
mantras.lit: You alone are Sandhyā and Sāvitrī; you, O Goddess, are the supreme mother. By you this universe is upheld; by you this world is created.
mantras.tr: You alone are the sacred twilight and the Sāvitrī verse; you, O Goddess, are the supreme Mother. By you this universe is sustained, and by you this world is brought forth.

comm.t: Brahmā continues identifying her with the forms of sacred worship — the twilight rite (Sandhyā) and the Sāvitrī verse recited in it — and then names her the supreme Mother, by whom the world is created and sustained.

Sandhyā and Sāvitrī belong together: the Sāvitrī (Gāyatrī) verse addressed to Savitṛ is recited at the twilight worship. To call the Goddess both is to make the daily Vedic observance itself her form. The verse then passes from ritual to cosmology: the one invoked at dawn and dusk is the mother of the world.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 422, सन्ध्या; 699, सावित्री; and 823, जननी.

mantras.anvaya: देवि, त्वया एतत् पाल्यते; अन्ते च सर्वदा त्वम् (एतत्) अत्सि। विसृष्टौ त्वं सृष्टिरूपा, पालने च स्थितिरूपा, …
mantras.anvaya_en: A passive sentence, an active one with an understood object (एतत्), and a series of nominal predicates with locatives of occasion, continued in 1.77 (संहृतिरूपा).
mantras.lit: By you this is protected, O Goddess, and you devour (it) at the end, always. In creation you have the form of creation, and the form of preservation in protecting,
mantras.tr: By you, O Goddess, it is protected, and at the end of every age you consume it. When the world is brought forth, you are its creation; while it is sustained, you are its preservation;
mantras.tr_note: सर्वदा ‘always’ with अन्ते is rendered ‘at the end of every age’: each dissolution, not one alone.

comm.t: The three cosmic works are given to her one after another: she protects the world, consumes it at every end, and in each phase takes the form of that phase — creation in creating, preservation in protecting. Dissolution follows in 1.77.

The three works ordinarily assigned to Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra are all hers; the speaker is Brahmā himself, the creator, who here says that creation is her form. The tradition reads this as the Devī Māhātmya’s central claim: the gods act through her power.

mantras.anvaya: जगन्मये, तथा अस्य जगतः अन्ते (त्वं) संहृतिरूपा। (त्वं) महाविद्या, महामाया, महामेधा, महास्मृतिः, …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the series of 1.76 (सृष्टिरूपा … स्थितिरूपा … संहृतिरूपा); the second begins a list of nominatives predicated of the Goddess, continued in 1.78.
mantras.lit: so too, at the end of this world, the form of dissolution, O you who consist of the world. (You are) the great knowledge, the great illusion, the great intelligence, the great memory,
mantras.tr: and at the end of this world, O you whose being is the world, you are its dissolution. You are the Great Knowledge and the Great Illusion, the Great Intelligence and the Great Memory,

comm.t: The triad of 1.76 is completed: at the world’s end she takes the form of its dissolution. Then begins a litany of ‘great’ names — knowledge, illusion, intelligence, memory. Two printing errors of the digital text are corrected in this verse (सिंहृति → संहृति, महास्मृतः → महास्मृतिः), both with the independent witnesses; see corrections.json.

Mahāvidyā and Mahāmāyā stand side by side, as liberation and bondage did in 1.57–58: the Goddess is both the knowledge that frees and the illusion that binds. ‘Great’ marks each as her cosmic form, not a human faculty.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 584, महाविद्या, and 215, महामाया, and the simple forms 538, मेधा, and 540, स्मृतिः.

mantras.anvaya: भवती च महामोहा, महादेवी, महासुरी। त्वं च सर्वस्य गुणत्रयविभाविनी प्रकृतिः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The list of 1.77 continues with भवती as its expressed subject; a second clause names her as Prakṛti, with सर्वस्य and an epithet.
mantras.lit: And Your Ladyship (is) the great delusion, the great Goddess, the great Asurī; and you are the primal nature of all, who brings forth the three guṇas.
mantras.tr: and Great Delusion, Great Goddess and mighty Asurī. You are the primal Nature of all things, unfolding the three qualities.

comm.t: The litany continues: she is the great delusion as well as the great knowledge of 1.77, the great Goddess, and — in the Gita Press reading — the great Asurī. She is also Prakṛti, the material source of everything, from which the three guṇas unfold.

The Sāṃkhya term prakṛti is taken over: matter and its three qualities (sattva, rajas, tamas) are not an inert principle opposed to spirit but the Goddess herself. The Gita Press pāṭha’s liturgical scheme, in which the three caritas are presided over by Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī, is often explained through these guṇas; that scheme is tradition, not stated in this verse.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 209, महादेवी; 397, मूलप्रकृतिः; and 763, त्रिगुणात्मिका.

mantras.anvaya: (त्वं) कालरात्रिः, महारात्रिः, दारुणा मोहरात्रिः च। त्वं श्रीः, त्वम् ईश्वरी, त्वं ह्रीः, त्वं बोधलक्षणा बुद्धिः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three ‘night’ names with one adjective, then four identity statements each with त्वम्.
mantras.lit: (You are) the Night of Time, the Great Night, and the dreadful Night of Delusion. You are Śrī, you are the Sovereign, you are Modesty, you are Understanding, whose mark is awareness.
mantras.tr: You are the Night of Time, the Great Night, the terrible Night of Delusion. You are Fortune, you are the Sovereign, you are Modesty, you are Understanding, whose very mark is awakening.

comm.t: Brahmā names her as three nights — of Time, the Great Night, and the dreadful night of delusion — and then as Fortune, Sovereignty, Modesty and Understanding. The dark and the auspicious are named in one breath. बोध ‘awakening’ in the last word echoes the purpose of the hymn, the awakening (विबोधन) of Viṣṇu (1.70).

The three nights are commonly explained as nights of dissolution and of delusion, though explanations of each differ and the text does not define them. Kālarātri is also one of the nine Durgās: the Devī Kavaca recited before the Gita Press pāṭha names her seventh (सप्तमं कालरात्रीति). Here ह्री is the virtue of modesty, paired with लज्जा in 1.80, not a seed-syllable.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 271, ईश्वरी, and describes her as 491, कालरात्र्यादिशक्त्यौघवृता, ‘surrounded by hosts of powers beginning with Kālarātri’ — there Kālarātri is one of her attendant powers, here one of her own names.

mantras.anvaya_en: A list of predicate nominatives with त्वम् and an understood असि, continuing the list of 1.77–79: first five virtues, then a run of feminine possessive adjectives naming her weapons.
mantras.lit: (You are) modesty, nourishment and likewise contentment; you (are) peace and forbearance too. (You are) sword-bearing, trident-bearing, terrible, mace-bearing and likewise discus-bearing;
mantras.tr: You are modesty, nourishment and contentment; you are peace, and patience too. You bear the sword and the trident; you are terrible; you carry the mace and the discus;

comm.t: Brahmā’s list turns in mid-verse from inner qualities to weapons. Modesty, nourishment, contentment, peace and forbearance are the gentlest powers of a person; the next line arms the same Goddess and calls her घोरा, ‘terrible’. The hymn makes no division between the two.

Several of these qualities return in the yā devī hymn of chapter 5 as forms in which the Devī abides in all beings: क्षान्ति (5.38-40), लज्जा (5.44-46), शान्ति (5.47-49) and तुष्टि (5.68-70). The weapons named in 1.80–81 match the dhyāna of Mahākālī that the Gita Press pāṭha sets before the first carita (sword, discus, mace, arrows, bow, iron club, trident, bhuśuṇḍī, a head, conch); the hymn names all of them except the head. The dhyāna is liturgical tradition, not part of the Purāṇa.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same names as single epithets: 443 तुष्टिः, 444 पुष्टिः, 447 शान्तिः and 740 लज्जा. The overlap is in vocabulary for the Goddess’s powers; the two texts are separate works.

samasa.type: prādi tatpuruṣa (the prefix अति ‘beyond, exceedingly’ as first member)
samasa.sense: surpassingly beautiful

morph.note: Comparative in -तर (taddhita) on सौम्य, feminine -तरा. The thing surpassed stands in the ablative: सौम्यतरा अशेषसौम्येभ्यः ‘gentler than all gentle things’.
Taddhita from सोम ‘the moon (Soma)’ with vṛddhi of the first syllable: ‘of the moon’s nature’, hence cool, mild, benign — the opposite of घोरा in 1.80.

mantras.anvaya: (त्वं) शङ्खिनी चापिनी बाणभुशुण्डीपरिघायुधा (असि)। सौम्या, अशेषसौम्येभ्यः सौम्यतरा, अतिसुन्दरी तु (असि)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The weapon-list of 1.80 ends; the second line sets a gentle triad against it. The ablative अशेषसौम्येभ्यः is taken with the comparative सौम्यतरा, which requires one. It can also be read with अतिसुन्दरी (‘more beautiful than all gentle things’); the comparative is the stronger claim on it.
mantras.lit: conch-bearing, bow-bearing, having arrows, bhuśuṇḍī and iron club as weapons; gentle, more gentle than all gentle things, and exceedingly beautiful.
mantras.tr: you bear the conch and the bow, and your weapons are arrows, the bhuśuṇḍī and the iron club. Yet you are gentle — gentler than every gentle thing — and beautiful beyond measure.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Yet’ renders the contrast the verse makes by placing सौम्या straight after the weapons; the Sanskrit has only तु ‘and, moreover’.

comm.t: The arming of the Goddess is completed — conch, bow, arrows, bhuśuṇḍī and iron club — and in the same breath she is called gentle, gentler than all gentle things, surpassingly beautiful. The terrible one of 1.80 (घोरा) and the gentle one here (सौम्या) are one.

The pairing of the fierce (घोर) and the gentle (सौम्य) is basic to the Śākta picture of the Goddess: the same Devī is worshipped in terrible and benign forms. This hymn states the pairing outright before the stories of chapters 2–13 show it in action.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has सौम्या as name 910. The adjective is common; the shared word shows a shared idiom of praise, not a borrowing.
A modern reflection: the hymn does not ask the reader to choose between a gentle and a fierce divinity. Protection and tenderness are offered as aspects of one care.

samasa.alt: पर and अपर can also be taken as the transcendent and the immanent (the supreme and the manifest), so ‘supreme over both the transcendent and the manifest’. The compound is the same dvandva either way.

samasa.sense: O you who are the self of everything — the same formation as स्वरात्मिका (1.73) and मात्रात्मिका (1.74)

morph.note: The interrogative किम् with the particle चित् becomes an indefinite: ‘anything’. With the relative यत् it generalises: यत् किंचित् ‘whatever at all’. क्वचित् (क्व ‘where?’ + चित्) is the adverb ‘anywhere’.
Vocative singular of an ā-stem feminine: the final ā becomes e (अखिलात्मिका → अखिलात्मिके), as in देवि from देवी with shortening.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) अखिलात्मिके, त्वम् एव परापराणां परमा परमेश्वरी (असि)। यत् च किंचित् सत् असत् वा वस्तु क्वचित् (अस्ति) —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is a complete statement. The second opens a relative clause (यत् … वस्तु) whose correlative तस्य सर्वस्य comes in 1.83.
mantras.lit: Of the higher and the lower the highest, you alone are the supreme Īśvarī. And whatever thing (there is) anywhere, existent or non-existent, O Self of all —
mantras.tr: Highest of all things high and low, you alone are the supreme Sovereign. And whatever thing there is, anywhere, whether it is or is not, O Soul of all —
mantras.tr_note: The second line is completed by 1.83 (‘of all that, you are the power’).

comm.t: Brahmā moves from listing names to a claim about everything: she is the highest over high and low alike, and the second line begins to say that whatever exists, or does not exist, belongs to her. The sentence finishes in 1.83.
सत् and असत् are often explained in Indian thought as the manifest (the effect) and the unmanifest (the cause). Read so, the verse leaves nothing, manifest or latent, outside the Goddess.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 790 परापरा, 396 परमेश्वरी and 661 सदसद्रूपधारिणी (‘bearing the forms of being and non-being’). The concepts are the same; the formulations belong to each text.
