samasa.alt: It can also be read as two words, जगत् (acc.) + स्रष्टा, with the agent noun taking an object like a verb, which keeps the line’s three जगत् parallel (creates / protects / devours the world). The sense is the same; the printed text joins all three, so print decides nothing.

morph.note: Passive present of √स्तु: the root vowel lengthens before the passive marker -य- (स्तू-य-), with the ātmanepada second-person ending -से. ‘Are you praised?’ — here rhetorical: ‘how can you be praised?’
√अद् (adādi) adds the ending directly to the root: अद् + ति → अत्ति, with d unvoiced before t.
स्रष्टृ ‘creator’ is the agent noun (tṛc) of √सृज्; nom. sg. स्रष्टा. The root’s vowel and r change places (सृज् → स्रष्) before the suffix.

mantras.anvaya: तस्य सर्वस्य या शक्तिः, सा त्वम् (असि)। तदा (त्वं) किं स्तूयसे? यया त्वया, यः जगत्स्रष्टा (यः) जगत् पाति (यः) जगत् अत्ति, (सः अपि निद्रावशं नीतः) —
mantras.anvaya_en: Line one completes 1.82 with the correlative pair या … सा. Line two opens a long relative clause: यया त्वया is the agent of नीतः in 1.84, and यः … जगत् describes the one who was put to sleep.
mantras.lit: Of all that, the power which (it has) — that (power) you (are). How then are you to be praised? By whom — by you — he who (is) the creator of the world, (who) protects the world, (who) devours the world,
mantras.tr: of all that, you are the power. How then can anyone praise you? You, by whom he who creates the world, sustains the world and devours the world
mantras.tr_note: The sentence continues into 1.84: ‘— even he has been brought under the sway of sleep’.

comm.t: The argument of the hymn is made plain: if she is the power (शक्ति) of everything that is, then every act — praise included — is already hers, and no praise can reach her. The second line names the one she has overcome: the god who creates, preserves and consumes the world, i.e. the sleeping Viṣṇu.

In Śākta thought śakti is the power by which any being acts, inseparable from it. The verse applies the idea to the gods themselves: even the agent of creation, preservation and destruction acts through her, and when she withdraws (as sleep) he does not act at all.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) gives the three acts to the Goddess directly: 264 सृष्टिकर्त्री (creator), 266 गोप्त्री (protector), 268 संहारिणी (destroyer). The Devī Māhātmya keeps them with a god and makes her the power behind him.
A modern reflection: the hymn admits its own limit. To say ‘how can you be praised?’ in the middle of praise is a way of keeping words honest about what they cannot hold.

Literally ‘master, lord’; with an infinitive it means ‘having power to’. The word picks up परमेश्वरी of 1.82: she is the Īśvarī, and no one is ईश्वर to praise her.

mantras.anvaya: सः अपि निद्रावशं नीतः। इह त्वां स्तोतुं कः ईश्वरः? विष्णुः, अहम्, ईशानः एव च शरीरग्रहणं (त्वया कारिताः) —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the relative clause of 1.83 (यया त्वया … सः अपि … नीतः) and asks a rhetorical question. The second line names three subjects whose verb, कारिताः, comes in 1.85.
mantras.lit: — even he has been led into the control of sleep. Who here is able to praise you? Viṣṇu, I and Īśāna too, (have been made by you to undertake) the taking of bodies —
mantras.tr: — even he has been brought under the sway of sleep. Who here has the power to praise you? Viṣṇu, I myself and Īśāna
mantras.tr_note: The second line continues into 1.85: ‘have been made by you to take on bodies’.

comm.t: The creator, preserver and consumer of the world lies asleep by her power, so no one is fit to praise her. Brahmā then names the three gods — Viṣṇu, himself and Īśāna (Śiva) — and in the next verse says that their very bodies are her doing.

Śākta readers take 1.84–85 as a foundation for the Goddess’s priority over the three gods: the three who create, preserve and dissolve are themselves made to take form by her. The speaker is Brahmā, one of the three, which gives the admission its weight.
A modern reflection: the most capable figures in the story are shown to depend on a power they did not make. The hymn turns the gods’ own testimony into a lesson in humility.

morph.note: Causative (णिच्) of √कृ, कारयति ‘makes (someone) do’, in the passive participle. In the passive of a causative the person made to act becomes the subject (विष्णुः, अहम्, ईशानः) and the thing done stays accusative (शरीरग्रहणम्). The plural masculine covers all three.

The enclitic ते is formally genitive or dative singular of युष्मद्. Purāṇic and epic verse use it with past participles for the agent, ‘by you’; a genitive of the agent with the participle is the grammatical explanation. Reading ते as the plural pronoun ‘they (were made)’ is also possible, but it sits awkwardly with अहम्.
Optative of possibility in a rhetorical question: कः … शक्तिमान् भवेत् ‘who could be able?’
Possessive -मत् on शक्ति; nom. sg. masculine -मान्. The word echoes शक्तिः of 1.83: she is the शक्ति of all, so who is शक्तिमान् to praise her?

mantras.anvaya: (विष्णुः अहम् ईशानः च शरीरग्रहणं) ते यतः कारिताः, अतः त्वां स्तोतुं कः शक्तिमान् भवेत्? (हे) देवि, सा त्वम् इत्थं स्वैः उदारैः प्रभावैः संस्तुता —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence begun in 1.84 with a यतः … अतः (‘since … therefore’) pair. The second line opens a new sentence: सा त्वम् … संस्तुता is the subject of the imperatives in 1.86.
mantras.lit: since (we) have been made by you (to take bodies), therefore who could be able to praise you? You, (such as you are), thus praised, O Devī, by (the telling of) your own exalted powers,
mantras.tr: have been made by you to take on bodily form — so who could have the power to praise you? O Devī, praised in this way for your own exalted powers,
mantras.tr_note: The first half finishes 1.84; the second half begins the request that 1.86 states.

comm.t: Brahmā ends the praise with its reason: the three gods owe even their bodies to her, so none of them can praise her adequately. The second line turns from praise to petition: ‘you, thus praised …’ leads straight into the request of 1.86.

The hymn closes in the classical manner of a stotra: an admission that praise falls short, then the request. Here the praise has been nothing but a recital of her own powers (प्रभावैः स्वैः) — she is praised with what is already hers.
A modern reflection: Brahmā asks only after acknowledging what he is. The order — recognition first, request second — is the shape of the whole hymn.

mantras.anvaya: (हे देवि) एतौ दुराधर्षौ असुरौ मधुकैटभौ मोहय। जगत्स्वामी अच्युतः च लघु प्रबोधं नीयताम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two requests: an active imperative to the Goddess (मोहय) and a passive imperative about Viṣṇu (नीयताम्), joined by च.
mantras.lit: delude these two hard-to-assail asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha; and let Acyuta, lord of the world, be brought quickly to waking,
mantras.tr: bewilder these two invincible asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and let Acyuta, the lord of the world, be woken quickly,

comm.t: The request at last: two things, one for each side. Delude the asuras; wake Viṣṇu. Both are acts of the same power — the Goddess as Mahāmāyā clouds the asuras’ minds and, as Yoganidrā, releases the god.

The dhyāna of Mahākālī in the Gita Press pāṭha sums up this scene: she is the one whom the lotus-born (Brahmā) praised, when Hari slept, for the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha (यामस्तौत्स्वपिते हरौ कमलजो हन्तुं मधुं कैटभम्). The dhyāna is liturgical, but it is drawn from these verses.
A modern reflection: the same power is asked both to confuse and to awaken. The text does not treat illusion and clarity as the work of rival powers.

mantras.tr: and let him be roused to slay these two great asuras.

comm.t: The last line of Brahmā’s hymn repeats the second request with a purpose added: wake him so that he may kill the two. प्रबोध (1.86) and बोध here may simply be the same waking said twice, or बोध may mean awareness — knowing what must be done; the text does not decide.

The hymn of Brahmā (1.73–87) is the first of the four great hymns of the Devī Māhātmya; the others come in chapters 4, 5 and 11. In the Śākta tradition it is recited as a hymn to the Goddess as Yoganidrā, the sleep of Viṣṇu.
A modern reflection: the hymn ends with a practical request. Its long praise serves an urgent need, and it says so plainly.

mantras.tr: Praised in this way by Brahmā, the Ordainer, the Goddess who is the dark power of sleep
mantras.tr_note: तामसी ‘of tamas’ is rendered ‘the dark power of sleep’ because in this scene she is Viṣṇu’s Yoganidrā (1.66, 1.69); the sentence runs on to 1.91.

comm.t: The hymn has its effect. Medhas names the Goddess here तामसी, ‘of tamas’: she is the dark, heavy power of sleep that holds Viṣṇu, the Yoganidrā Brahmā has just praised.

The Gita Press pāṭha assigns the first carita to Mahākālī as presiding deity (its viniyoga and dhyāna); that assignment is liturgical tradition. तामसी is the word in the Purāṇa’s own text that the assignment most naturally connects with: the first manifestation is the Goddess under the guṇa of tamas.

Ablative singular of the s-stem उरस् ‘chest’. It is left outside the dvandva, joined by तथा — a common way of completing a list in verse.

mantras.anvaya: (सा देवी) विष्णोः प्रबोधनार्थाय मधुकैटभौ निहन्तुं (च) नेत्रास्यनासिकाबाहुहृदयेभ्यः तथा उरसः (निर्गम्य) —
mantras.anvaya_en: Two expressions of purpose and two ablatives of separation; the absolutive निर्गम्य that governs the ablatives comes at the start of 1.91.
mantras.lit: for the sake of awakening Viṣṇu, to slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha, from (his) eyes, mouth, nose, arms and heart, and likewise from (his) chest
mantras.tr: so that Viṣṇu might wake and slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha, came forth from his eyes, mouth, nose, arms and heart, and from his breast,
mantras.tr_note: ‘Came forth’ is supplied from निर्गम्य at the start of 1.91; ‘his’ (Viṣṇu’s) is understood.

comm.t: The Goddess grants both requests of the hymn. She withdraws from Viṣṇu’s body, limb by limb — eyes, mouth, nose, arms, heart, chest — so that he wakes, and wakes in order to kill the two asuras.
Brahmā had praised her as dwelling in Hari’s eyes (हरिनेत्रकृतालयाम्, 1.70); the eyes stand first here as she leaves. Sleep is pictured as a presence in the body that departs by every organ.

mantras.anvaya: (सा) निर्गम्य अव्यक्तजन्मनः ब्रह्मणः दर्शने तस्थौ। तया मुक्तः जगन्नाथः जनार्दनः च उत्तस्थौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses joined by च, each ending in the perfect of √स्था — तस्थौ (she stood) and उत्तस्थौ (he rose).
mantras.lit: having come out, (she) stood in the sight of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest. And Janārdana, lord of the world, released by her, rose up
mantras.tr: and stood before the eyes of Brahmā, whose birth is beyond knowing. Released by her, Janārdana, lord of the world, rose
mantras.tr_note: ‘Came forth’ was given in 1.90; the verse continues into 1.92 (‘from his serpent couch on the one ocean’).

comm.t: Two movements answer each other: she comes out and stands where Brahmā can see her (तस्थौ), and Viṣṇu, freed, rises (उत्तस्थौ). The Goddess praised in the hymn is now visible to the one who praised her.

Medhas had said that the Goddess, though eternal, is spoken of as ‘born’ whenever she appears for the gods’ work (1.65–66). This is the first such appearance: not a birth, but a coming forth from where she already was.

mantras.tr: from his serpent couch on the one ocean. Then he saw the two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, evil-hearted and of surpassing strength and prowess,

comm.t: Viṣṇu rises from Śeṣa on the cosmic waters and, for the first time, sees the two asuras who were about to kill Brahmā. The verse sets the scene of the fight: one ocean, no land.

mantras.anvaya: (सः) विभुः बाहुप्रहरणः पञ्च वर्षसहस्राणि (ताभ्यां युयुधे)। अतिबलोन्मत्तौ महामायाविमोहितौ तौ अपि (केशवम् उक्तवन्तौ) —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes 1.93 (‘fought … for five thousand years’); the second gives the subject of a new sentence whose verb, उक्तवन्तौ, comes in 1.95.
mantras.lit: for five thousands of years, the all-pervading one, with his arms as weapons. And those two, maddened by excessive strength, deluded by Mahāmāyā,
mantras.tr: for five thousand years, the all-pervading Lord fighting with his bare arms. Then the two, drunk with their own great strength and deluded by Mahāmāyā,

comm.t: The battle lasts five thousand years, Viṣṇu fighting with his arms alone, and is not decided by force. It turns when Mahāmāyā clouds the asuras’ minds — the first of Brahmā’s requests (1.86) fulfilled.
The compound महामायाविमोहितौ takes up Medhas’s teaching: Mahāmāyā draws even the minds of the wise into delusion (1.55–56). The asuras are her first example in the stories.

mantras.tr: said to Keśava, “Choose a boon from us.”
mantras.tr_note: The passive ‘let a boon be chosen’ is rendered as an active imperative.

comm.t: The delusion shows itself as pride: after five thousand years of combat the asuras, pleased with their opponent, offer him a boon — as though they were the gods and he the petitioner.
The reversal is the point the tradition draws: a boon is a superior’s gift. In offering one to Viṣṇu the asuras act out the confusion that Mahāmāyā has worked in them (1.94).

mantras.anvaya: (यतः युवाम्) अद्य मे तुष्टौ, (अतः) उभौ अपि मम वध्यौ भवेताम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A single optative clause; तुष्टौ is circumstantial (‘since you are pleased’), and the anvaya spells out the implied reason. Alternatively भवेताम् can be supplied twice: ‘may you be pleased with me; may you both be slain by me’.
mantras.lit: (Since you are) pleased with me today, may you both be (persons) to be slain by me.
mantras.tr: If you are pleased with me, then let both of you be slain by me today.
mantras.tr_note: The participle तुष्टौ is rendered as a condition (‘if you are pleased’); the Sanskrit states it without a conjunction.

comm.t: Viṣṇu accepts the offer and asks the one thing that ends the war: that both asuras be killable by him. Their own boon becomes the instrument of their death.

The motif of a boon turned against the giver recurs in the Purāṇas. Here it carries the chapter’s teaching: the asuras are undone not by Viṣṇu’s strength, which five thousand years did not make decisive, but by the delusion of Mahāmāyā.

mantras.anvaya_en: A rhetorical question and a statement; हि gives the reason (‘for this much is my choice’).
mantras.lit: What (use is there) here of another boon? For this much (is) chosen by me.
mantras.tr: What need have I of any other boon? This alone is my choice.

comm.t: Viṣṇu closes off any bargaining: he wants nothing else. The asuras, bound by their offer, cannot refuse.
The hiatus अत्र | एतावत् falls at the pāda break and is printed so in the Gita Press text; it is a licence of epic verse, not an error, and is kept.

mantras.anvaya: इति वञ्चिताभ्यां (ताभ्यां) तदा सर्वं जगत् आपोमयं (विलोक्य) —
mantras.anvaya_en: A participial agent phrase and the object of an absolutive; the absolutive विलोक्य and the passive verb गदितः come in 1.101.
mantras.lit: By the two, thus deceived, then — the whole world (being) made of water —
mantras.tr: Thus deceived, the two then looked and saw the whole world turned to water,
mantras.tr_note: ‘Looked and saw’ is supplied from विलोक्य at the start of 1.101; the instrumental agent is rendered as the subject.

comm.t: The asuras realise they have been caught by their own word. Looking about for a way out, they see that the whole world is water — the cosmic flood on which Viṣṇu slept (1.66–67).

Who deceived them is left implicit: by Viṣṇu’s taking them at their word, and behind that by Mahāmāyā, who had bewildered them (1.94). The narrative makes the deception the Goddess’s work, done through the god.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes 1.100 with a passive main verb (गदितः); the second is the asuras’ words, a command with a relative clause of place (यत्र … न).
mantras.lit: having looked, the lotus-eyed Blessed One was addressed by the two: ‘Slay us where the earth is not flooded with water.’
mantras.tr: and they said to the lotus-eyed Lord, “Slay us where the earth is not flooded with water.”
mantras.tr_note: The passive (‘was addressed by the two’) is rendered actively.

comm.t: The asuras try to slip their promise: since the whole world is water, a place ‘where the earth is not flooded’ seems not to exist. They grant the boon on a condition they think cannot be met.

The Purāṇa recension (the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa as edited in GRETIL) has further lines after this verse that the Gita Press text does not carry; this edition follows the Gita Press 700 and adds nothing (see corrections.json, recension notes).

Absolutive of √वच् with samprasāraṇa (व → उ) and k for c: उक्त्वा ‘having said’. With कृत्वा it gives two steps before the main act.

Neuter dual of शिरस्: nominative and accusative are the same (शिरसी), so the one word serves both as the object of कृत्वा (‘having placed their heads’) and the subject of छिन्ने (‘the heads were cut off’). A neuter dual in -ī (like छिन्ने in -e) is pragṛhya and would stand unjoined before a vowel (ईदूदेद्द्विवचनं प्रगृह्यम्, 1.1.11); here a consonant follows, so no question of sandhi arises.

mantras.anvaya: ‘तथा’ इति उक्त्वा, शङ्खचक्रगदाभृता भगवता तयोः शिरसी जघने कृत्वा चक्रेण वै छिन्ने।
mantras.anvaya_en: A passive sentence: the subject शिरसी with its verb छिन्ने, the agent भगवता, and two absolutives (उक्त्वा, कृत्वा) sharing that agent. शिरसी does double duty as the object of कृत्वा.
mantras.lit: Having said ‘So (be it)’, by the Blessed One, bearer of conch, discus and mace, having placed (them) on (his) loins, the two heads of the two were indeed cut off with the discus.
mantras.tr: Saying “So be it,” the Lord who bears the conch, the discus and the mace laid them on his lap and cut off their two heads with his discus.
mantras.tr_note: The passive is rendered actively. जघन, properly the hips or loins, is rendered ‘lap’: the one place above the water.

comm.t: Viṣṇu meets the condition exactly: the only ground not covered by water is his own body. He lays their heads on his lap and cuts them off with the discus. The asuras die by the terms of their own boon.

The narrative turns the asuras’ cleverness against them, as the boon itself was turned (1.97). The cause, as the chapter has insisted, is Mahāmāyā’s delusion rather than force: five thousand years of fighting did not end the war, a confusion of mind did.
A modern reflection: the asuras look for a loophole in the world and find none outside the one they are fighting. The story leaves no place that is not within the Lord’s reach.

mantras.anvaya: एवम् एषा (देवी) स्वयं ब्रह्मणा संस्तुता समुत्पन्ना। अस्याः देव्याः प्रभावं तु भूयः शृणु, (अहं) ते वदामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: A closing summary (एवम् … समुत्पन्ना), then the transition to the next story: an imperative and a first-person present.
mantras.lit: Thus she arose, praised by Brahmā himself. But hear further the power of this Goddess; I tell (it) to you.
mantras.tr: So it was that she appeared, praised by Brahmā himself. Now hear more of this Goddess’s power; I shall tell you.
mantras.tr_note: स्वयम् is taken with ब्रह्मणा (‘by Brahmā himself’). It can also be taken with the subject: ‘she appeared of her own accord’.

comm.t: Medhas closes the first story and opens the next. The ring is complete: he had said that the eternal Goddess is called ‘born’ (उत्पन्ना) when she appears for the gods’ purpose (1.65–66); now he says एवम् एषा समुत्पन्ना — ‘this is how she arose’. शृणु and ते are singular: he speaks to the king.

This is the last mantra of chapter 1. In the Gita Press pāṭha it is followed by the bījas ऐं ॐ, closing the sampuṭa that ॐ ऐं opened in 1.1; they belong to the recitation, not to the Purāṇa. The colophon names the chapter मधुकैटभवधः, the Slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the first carita, which the pāṭha assigns to Mahākālī.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has a name for a goddess praised by the gods, 83 ब्रह्मोपेन्द्रमहेन्द्रादिदेवसंस्तुतवैभवा, ‘whose glory is praised by Brahmā, Upendra, Mahendra and the other gods’. The motif is shared; the Devī Māhātmya has just told one such praise in full.

flags.uncertain: स्वयम् may qualify ब्रह्मणा (‘by Brahmā himself’, chosen) or the Goddess (‘she arose of her own accord’); both readings are grammatical.
